title: One key, two equality representations
stem: A map treats strings case-insensitively but hashes their original character codes. Explain a failure with `"Map"` and `"map"`, and specify a correct contract without claiming collision-free hashing.
solution: Those two keys are equal under the map's declared equality, so both must follow the same home and probe route. Original-case hashes can send them to different buckets, making lookup miss an equal existing key or creating duplicates. Hash the same normalized representation used by equality, for example the specified case-folded character sequence. Keep that normalization consistent for insertion, query and deletion. Different normalized strings may still collide; compare actual normalized keys within the bucket or route. The corrected implication is equality implies equal hash, never equal hash implies equality. Changing normalization while records are stored requires rebuilding.

title: Signed remainder and overflow
stem: At capacity 11, compute normalized homes for $-1,-12,-999$. Explain why `abs(key) % 11` differs and why it can fail at the minimum signed integer.
solution: Write each key as $11q+r$ with $0\le r<11$. The residues are ten, ten and two because $-999=11(-91)+2$. Absolute-value reduction gives one, one and nine, which are valid indices but a different hash mapping. In a fixed-width signed type, the negative endpoint has no representable positive counterpart; taking its absolute value can overflow or retain a negative result. Instead compute a remainder safely and add capacity when that remainder is negative. This normalizes the mathematical modulo without negating the original key. Every operation must use the same convention.

title: Strides and attainable homes
stem: Keys are $5+18t$, with $t=0,\ldots,19$, at capacity 24. How many distinct homes can they reach? Give the homes and explain the correct greatest-common-divisor argument.
solution: The residue difference is always a multiple of 18. A repeat occurs when $24$ divides $18d$, whose smallest positive solution is $d=24/\gcd(18,24)=4$. Starting at five gives homes five, 23, 17 and 11, then repeats. Each receives five of the twenty keys. The table's overall load is $20/24$, but only four buckets receive entries. Primality is irrelevant to the argument actually used here: the cycle is determined by the greatest common divisor. A capacity relatively prime to the stride would yield a full residue cycle, while still not proving randomness for other datasets.

title: Horner arithmetic with a degenerate base
stem: Evaluate codes $[1,2,3]$ with base five modulo 17. Then compare codes $[1,3,2]$ when the base is 18 modulo 17, and explain what information that base loses.
solution: For base five, the successive prefix residues are $1$, $5(1)+2=7$, and $5(7)+3=38\equiv4$. The expanded polynomial is $1(25)+2(5)+3=38$, giving the same result. Base 18 is congruent to one modulo 17, so every positional power is one; both sequences have residue $1+2+3=6$. This preserves a character sum but discards ordering information. The recurrence's correctness follows by prefix induction, yet a mathematically correct recurrence can implement a poor hash. Speed, valid indices and useful distribution are separate properties.

title: A finite-word polynomial collision
stem: Two length-two code blocks have base-31 polynomial values 2112. Prove that any concatenation of $r$ such blocks gives the same hash for all $2^r$ choices, including word-overflow reduction. State the resulting string length.
solution: Appending a two-code block transforms a prefix hash $v$ into $31^2v+2112$. The transformation is identical for either block, so induction on the number of appended blocks makes every choice sequence produce the same result. Reducing each update modulo $2^w$ preserves equality, so intentional finite-word overflow does not remove this collision. There are $2^r$ block-choice strings if the blocks differ, but each has length $2r$, not $r$. This constructive collision family shows that deterministic polynomial hashing does not provide a universal protection against inputs chosen after the function is known.

title: A decision-tree boundary
stem: A dictionary has 255 keys and binary comparison-only tests. Give the least possible decision-tree height needed to distinguish all present-key outputs and absence, then explain why arithmetic hashing does not contradict it.
solution: There are at least 256 distinct terminal outputs. A binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves, so $h\ge8$. This is a necessary bound for the specified comparison model; it does not by itself construct an optimal dictionary. Hashing uses arithmetic on key bits and indexed memory access, allowing distinctions that are not limited to binary comparison branches. Therefore a constant expected slot-access claim changes the permitted operations rather than violating this lower bound. If string length is unbounded, hashing still has to account for the cost of reading the key representation.

title: An immutable-key requirement
stem: A key with field value 12 is stored at $h(k)=k\bmod7$. Its field is changed to 13 without removing the entry. Explain the broken invariant and a reliable repair.
solution: The entry was stored in bucket five or a probe route starting there. The new field value makes equality and hashing use home six. A query for the mutated key can inspect bucket six and fail even though the object remains physically stored elsewhere. Accidental collisions could conceal the bug, so failure is not universal for every hash or capacity. Remove the entry while its original representation still determines the old route, then insert the new representation, or rebuild the table from the live objects. Prefer immutable equality-relevant fields so that stored placement and future lookup remain consistent.

title: Constant slot work versus string work
stem: Every query hashes a fresh length-$L$ string and inspects an expected two bucket records. Give a justified total complexity, including the case of a fingerprint collision requiring full equality.
solution: Horner hashing reads $L$ codes, so it already costs $\Theta(L)$. If two expected record comparisons can each inspect up to $L$ characters, expected total character work is bounded by a constant multiple of $L$, assuming the expected record count is independent of any unbounded comparison cost or using the uniform worst-case $O(L)$ bound. Thus total expected work is $O(L)$ and at least $\Omega(L)$ for fresh full-string hashing. Cached record fingerprints reject mismatches cheaply but do not remove the query's initial hash cost, nor justify accepting equal fingerprints as equal strings. The slot-access statement and total runtime are different measures.

title: Constant hash and map insertion
stem: All $n$ distinct keys hash to one chained bucket. Compare total cost of ordinary map insertion with inserting records promised distinct using unconditional head insertion. State what changes in the contract.
solution: Ordinary `put` scans the current chain to rule out an existing equal key. The successive failed equality counts are $0,1,\ldots,n-1$, summing to $n(n-1)/2$, plus linear total linking/hash work. The total is quadratic. If the caller guarantees distinctness and the implementation omits duplicate checks, each head insertion has constant pointer work and the total is linear. It is a different precondition, not an improvement of arbitrary map `put`. Future lookup still has a linear worst case in the single bucket. A multimap may intentionally allow duplicates and also avoid uniqueness search, but changes the data abstraction.

title: Nullable values and absence
stem: A table returns `null` from `get` both when a key is absent and when its stored value is null. Why can a two-sum implementation using this result be wrong? Specify the interface change.
solution: Membership and value retrieval are different questions. A present complement whose value is null would be mistaken for absence, possibly causing a valid pair to be missed or a duplicate record to be inserted. Return a presence flag separately, provide `contains`, or reserve a value that the contract explicitly forbids storing. The collision strategy cannot repair an ambiguous API. When two-sum uses a set, the relevant result is whether a prior position with that value exists. The query must occur before adding the current position, so a single occurrence cannot pair with itself.

title: Exact head-insertion chains
stem: Insert $[12,26,5,15,2,19,43]$ into seven buckets using floor-modulo and head insertion. Give all nonempty chains, the longest chain, and the number of collision pairs.
solution: Homes are five, five, five, one, two, five and one. Reversing the insertion order within each bucket gives bucket five $[19,5,26,12]$, bucket one $[43,15]$, and bucket two $[2]$. Four is the maximum chain length. Pair collisions are $\binom42+\binom22+\binom12=6+1+0=7$. Overflow entries are instead $(4-1)+(2-1)+(1-1)=4$. These two collision measures should not be substituted for one another. The chain ordering also determines exact successful-search ranks, so a tail-insertion answer would represent a different policy.

title: A fixed-table successful average
stem: For Q11's table, equally likely stored-key queries scan from each chain head. Compute the exact average comparisons and compare it with average bucket length.
solution: The four-entry chain contributes $1+2+3+4=10$, the two-entry chain contributes three, and the singleton contributes one. Total successful comparisons over the seven possible keys are 14, giving average two. Average bucket length is $7/7=1$. These quantities differ because successful queries choose records, making longer buckets more likely, and because a successful scan includes the matching comparison. The exact average follows from the actual chain lengths, not a universal probabilistic theorem. Head versus tail order can change individual-key ranks while leaving this equally likely all-key total unchanged.

title: A fixed-table miss distribution
stem: In Q11, a miss has probability one-half of selecting bucket five, one-quarter bucket one and one-quarter an empty bucket. Compute its expected entry comparisons and explain why $n/m$ is not the answer.
solution: A miss scans its entire selected chain. The expected comparisons are $(1/2)4+(1/4)2+(1/4)0=5/2$. The arithmetic load is one, but the query distribution favors crowded buckets, so it does not sample all buckets uniformly. Hash computation and accessing the bucket pointer add constant work separately. Under uniformly chosen home buckets, a miss would average one record comparison for this fixed table. Stating “average chain length equals one” without defining how a query selects a chain cannot justify the cost of a biased workload.

title: Bucket lengths and pair counts
stem: A chained table has bucket lengths $[0,4,1,3,0,2]$. Compute live load, occupied buckets, overflow entries, pair collisions and equally likely successful comparisons.
solution: The live count is ten and capacity six, so load is $5/3$. Four buckets are nonempty and overflow entries total $10-4=6$. Pair collisions total $6+0+3+1=10$. Successful comparisons total $10+1+6+3=20$, so the average is two. The identity $\sum_j\ell_j^2=\sum_j\ell_j+2\sum_j\binom{\ell_j}{2}$ gives squared sum $10+20=30$, which also yields $(30+10)/(2\cdot10)=2$. This provides an independent arithmetic check. Chaining permits load above one; applying an open-addressing fullness rule here would be incorrect.

title: Success-weighted size bias
stem: A table has one chain of length 20 and eighty empty buckets. Compare average bucket length with the expected chain length seen by a uniformly chosen stored key. Then compute the expected successful scan rank.
solution: There are 81 buckets and 20 records, so average bucket length is $20/81$. Every stored key belongs to the only nonempty chain, hence its selected chain length is exactly 20. Its equally likely successful position has average rank $(1+20)/2=10.5$. The small bucket average cannot bound stored-key search cost. More generally, the record-selected expected bucket length is $\sum_j\ell_j^2/n$, whereas the bucket-selected mean is $n/m$. This is a concrete demonstration of size bias. A uniform-home probabilistic model would need to justify why this configuration is unlikely, not deny that it exists.

title: Expected occupied buckets
stem: Five independent keys choose uniformly among eight buckets. Compute expected occupied and empty buckets exactly, without treating occupancy indicators as independent.
solution: A specified bucket is empty with probability $(7/8)^5=16807/32768$. Summing the eight empty indicators gives expected empty count $16807/4096$. Expected occupied count is eight minus that value, $15961/4096$, approximately 3.897. The indicators across buckets are dependent because the fixed five keys constrain total occupancy, but linearity of expectation still applies. The expected number of overflow entries is five minus expected occupied count, $4519/4096$. That is not the same as expected collision-pair count $\binom52/8=5/4$, which counts multiple pairs within longer buckets.

title: Fixed-bucket variance
stem: Under independent uniform homes, $n=48,m=12$. Give one specified bucket's expected length and variance. Does this prove that every bucket has exactly four entries?
solution: Each key contributes an independent Bernoulli indicator of probability $1/12$. The bucket length is binomial with mean $48/12=4$ and variance $48(1/12)(11/12)=11/3$. Positive variance immediately rules out a deterministic length of four. Different buckets are also not independent because their counts sum to 48. A theorem about maximum load or simultaneous concentration requires additional analysis; it cannot be inferred from the mean alone. An exact query in a displayed table should use that table's lengths, while an expectation question can use this specified random model.

title: Successful chaining expectation
stem: Thirty distinct keys are independently hashed to ten buckets and inserted at chain tails. A uniformly chosen stored key is queried. Derive expected successful entry comparisons exactly.
solution: For the $j$th inserted key, earlier colliding keys precede it. Each of the $j-1$ earlier keys collides with probability $1/10$, so expected rank is $1+(j-1)/10$. Average these ranks over the thirty equally likely stored keys: $1+(1/30)(0+1+\cdots+29)/10=1+29/20=49/20$. The result is 2.45 comparisons, including the match but excluding hashing. Head insertion reverses which later collisions precede each key yet gives the same all-key expectation. A biased query distribution or self-organizing chains can change it. Universal bucket-size bounds alone do not automatically provide this exact equality.

title: Sorted array buckets
stem: A bucket contains $r$ ordered keys in a contiguous growable array. Explain the worst-case costs of search, inserting a new smallest key, and deleting a middle key. Distinguish comparisons from moves.
solution: Binary search finds a key or insertion location using $O(\log r)$ comparisons. Inserting the new smallest key shifts all $r$ live records one position, giving $\Theta(r)$ moves even without a capacity change. A resize can add further linear copying but does not change that worst-case order. Deleting a middle entry shifts roughly half the remaining records and also takes $\Theta(r)$ moves. Therefore logarithmic location search does not make updates logarithmic. If the bucket were a balanced tree, a different representation could support logarithmic updates, but its pointer and balancing costs would need their own analysis.

title: Best bucket ordering for a biased workload
stem: A three-key chain is queried with probabilities $1/2,1/3,1/6$. Determine the least possible expected successful comparisons and prove that decreasing-probability order is optimal.
solution: Put the keys in decreasing probability order. The expectation is $(1/2)1+(1/3)2+(1/6)3=5/3$. For two positions $i<j$ containing probabilities $p<q$, swapping them changes expected cost by $(qi+pj)-(pi+qj)=(q-p)(i-j)<0$. Any inversion therefore increases cost; repeatedly removing inversions yields decreasing-probability order. This does not alter bucket membership or key uniqueness. Maintaining an estimated frequency ordering has update overhead and may respond poorly to changing workloads, so the static optimality proof is not a free constant-time implementation claim.

title: Pair expectation versus a per-query expectation
stem: Twenty fixed distinct keys use independent uniform homes in ten buckets. Compute expected total collision pairs, expected colliders of one absent query, and expected bucket size of one present key.
solution: There are 190 unordered pairs, each with collision probability one-tenth, so expected pair count is 19. An absent fixed query has twenty potential colliders, giving expected count two. A present key always counts itself plus 19 potential other colliders, giving expected bucket size $1+19/10=2.9$. The three quantities are different because their indicator sums have different index sets. The pair expectation is of order $n^2/m$, while a query's bucket work is of order $n/m$. Conflating a pair's probability $1/m$ with the expectation of all pairs is the central trap in the authentic doctoral question.

title: Exact birthday probability
stem: Four independent keys choose uniformly among eight buckets. Compute the exact probability of at least one pair collision and compare it with the expected number of pairs.
solution: The no-collision probability is $(8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot5)/8^4=105/256$. Its complement is $151/256$, approximately 0.589844. Expected pair count is $\binom42/8=3/4$. These do not coincide: outcomes with multiple collisions contribute more than one to the pair count but only one to the collision-event indicator. The union bound gives collision probability at most $3/4$, consistent with the exact result. The birthday exponential estimate would be $1-e^{-3/4}$, which is an approximation and should not replace the requested exact fraction.

title: Birthday memory scaling
stem: Use a union bound to give a sufficient capacity ensuring collision probability at most $0.01$ for 100 fixed keys with universal hashing. Explain whether the bound needs independent outputs.
solution: There are $\binom{100}{2}=4950$ pairs. Universal hashing bounds each pair's collision probability by $1/m$. The union bound therefore gives probability of any collision at most $4950/m$. A sufficient choice is $m\ge495000$. No independence between pair events is required for this bound. It is sufficient rather than necessary and can be loose. The much smaller capacity used by ordinary chained tables permits collisions while keeping individual expected query work low; insisting on almost no collisions solves a stronger requirement than efficient lookup.

title: A universal-family enumeration
stem: For prime seven, capacity three and keys zero and two, enumerate the collision fraction in the family with $a\in\{1,\ldots,6\}$ and $b\in\{0,\ldots,6\}$. Derive it from residue-class sizes.
solution: The affine map gives all 42 ordered pairs of distinct residues equally likely for these two distinct keys. Modulo-three classes within $0,\ldots,6$ have sizes three, two and two. Colliding ordered distinct pairs count $3(2)+2(1)+2(1)=10$. The fraction is $10/42=5/21$, below $1/3$. It is not exactly $1/3$, because the intermediate prime range is not a multiple of the final capacity and the two intermediate residues must differ. This calculation checks the bijection proof without assuming independent intermediate outputs, which would incorrectly include equal residues.

title: A restricted-parameter counterexample
stem: Keys are $\{0,1,2\}$, prime modulus seven and final capacity two. Restrict affine parameters to $a\in\{1,2\}$ and $b\in\{0,1,2\}$. Is this family universal? Exhibit a violating pair.
solution: Choose keys zero and two. Before final reduction their affine outputs differ by $2a$, and with the specified ranges neither pair wraps modulo seven: zero maps to $b$ and two to $2a+b\le6$. Both outputs therefore have the same parity for every one of the six parameter choices. Collision probability is one, exceeding $1/2$. The family is not universal. The standard theorem chooses parameters across the full prime field, not just the smaller key universe. This explicit counterexample explains why changing parameter ranges invalidates the ordered-residue bijection and must not be treated as a harmless notational variation.

title: Pairwise bounds without independence
stem: A universal family hashes 60 fixed keys into 20 buckets. Bound expected colliders of an absent fixed query. Can you infer a binomial distribution for its bucket length from universality alone?
solution: Sum sixty collision indicators, each with expectation at most $1/20$, giving expected colliders at most three. Including hashing and the bucket access yields $O(1+3)$ expected unit-cost work for a complete failed scan. Universality does not assert that these indicators are independent or have exactly probability $1/20$, so a binomial distribution is not justified. It supports a first-moment bound through linearity of expectation. A tail bound can be obtained from Markov using that moment, but the stronger concentration conclusions of independent uniform homes require additional assumptions.

title: A Markov tail bound
stem: In Q26, bound the probability an absent query encounters at least 30 colliding records. Compare that statement with a guaranteed maximum chain length.
solution: Let $X$ be the nonnegative collider count with $E[X]\le3$. Markov's inequality gives $\Pr(X\ge30)\le3/30=1/10$. This bounds a particular fixed query over random function selection; it is not a deterministic maximum-chain guarantee, nor an automatic bound for a query chosen adaptively after observing the table. To control many fixed queries simultaneously, a union bound would introduce their count and could be loose. A sampled function can still produce a bad table. Expected constant lookup permits rare expensive outcomes and must not be restated as a worst-case guarantee.

title: Choosing a function once
stem: An implementation randomly resamples the hash function at each operation without rebuilding. Explain why expected collision performance does not rescue its lookup correctness.
solution: An inserted key is placed according to the function chosen for insertion. A later query using a different function can begin at a different bucket or probe route and report absence. Correct placement depends on a stable table-lifetime function, not merely on each separately sampled function having a good distribution. Sample once when creating a table; retain the parameters with the table; resample only while relocating every live record during rebuilding. Probability analysis assumes that placement and lookup share the chosen function. Randomness can improve expected collisions but cannot replace the representation invariant that makes retrieval meaningful.

title: Collision pairs from a squared sum
stem: Bucket lengths sum to 18 and their squared sum is 54. Determine exact collision pairs and equally likely successful chained comparisons.
solution: Use $\ell^2=\ell+2\binom\ell2$ in each bucket and sum. Pair count is $(54-18)/2=18$. Successful comparison totals are $\sum\ell(\ell+1)/2=(54+18)/2=36$, giving average two over eighteen keys. These exact identities require no randomness and work for any valid nonnegative bucket lengths. The mean selected bucket length for a uniform stored key is $54/18=3$, so its average scan rank is $(3+1)/2=2$. This links size bias, collision counts and search costs while keeping each quantity distinct.

title: An adaptive-input limitation
stem: After a public deterministic division hash is chosen, an adversary selects $n$ keys. Construct a worst case at capacity $m$ and explain why a universal-family expected theorem with fixed keys does not directly cover this adaptive selection.
solution: Select $r,r+m,\ldots,r+(n-1)m$ within a sufficiently large allowed universe. Every key has home $r$, producing a chain of length $n$ or a linear-probing cluster. A universal-family proof averages over the function while holding the input set fixed independently of the sampled function. Here the chosen keys depend on that function, so the order of quantifiers changes and the theorem cannot simply be invoked. Secret randomized hashing or adversarially robust structures need additional analysis. The counterexample does not claim every practical randomized implementation is vulnerable; it identifies the missing assumption in the proposed argument.

title: Circular linear-probing insertion
stem: Insert $[10,21,32,43,9]$ into eleven empty slots using linear probing. Give every destination and probe count, then search for absent 54.

Total insertion probes are eleven. Absent 54 shares home ten and visits ten, zero, one, two and the first empty slot three, so it requires five probes. A diagram that splits the run at the physical array boundary can conceal the wraparound; logically the cluster is nine, ten, zero, one, two. The terminating empty cell is counted as a probe but not as a live unequal-key comparison.

title: Exact miss average for a circular run

title: Two tables with the same load
stem: Capacity is twelve and six slots are occupied. Table A has one circular run of six. Table B has six isolated occupied slots. Compare exact uniform-home miss probes and explain the difference.

title: Cluster attraction probabilities
stem: A capacity-twelve table has runs of lengths four and two, each followed by a distinct empty slot. A new absent key's home is uniform. What are the probabilities that insertion lands in those two terminating empty slots?
solution: A run's terminating empty slot receives the insertion when the home is any of the run's occupied positions or that empty position itself. The four-run therefore contributes five home choices and probability $5/12$; the two-run contributes three and probability $3/12$. Other empty positions receive their direct home probabilities. Empty destination slots are not uniformly likely, even though homes are uniform. Once a terminating slot is filled, its run grows and may merge with another run if adjacent. This positive feedback is primary clustering and explains why the random-permutation miss bound cannot simply be applied to linear probing.

title: Tombstone reachability

If zero is cleared to `EMPTY`, the search for 32 incorrectly stops after two probes, because the deleted position was occupied when 32 was displaced to one. The representation invariant is broken despite the live count being correct. A valid deletion either preserves a nonempty marker or repairs all affected linear-probing survivors before exposing a completed table state.

title: Updating past a tombstone
stem: After Q35's valid deletion, put key 32 with a new value. Give the correct probe route and count changes; show the duplicate bug caused by inserting immediately at the deleted slot.
solution: Start at home ten, inspect its unequal live key, remember the deleted slot zero, then find existing 32 at slot one. Replace its value there. Live count remains four and deleted count remains one. If insertion stops at zero, a second live 32 is created while the original remains at one, violating the map's uniqueness contract. A new key may collide with existing second-level placement; the original construction's acceptance tests did not include it. Supporting arbitrary dynamic insertion therefore requires rebuilding affected structure or a separately analyzed dynamic-perfect scheme. Worst-case constant slot lookup after successful static construction is a distinct claim from dynamic update costs or full-universe injectivity.

title: Geometric trial expectation
stem: Every independent perfect-hashing trial succeeds with probability at least one-half. Bound expected trials and the probability more than six trials are needed. Explain how lack of fresh randomness changes the conclusion.
solution: With success probability $p\ge1/2$, the expected geometric trial count is $1/p\le2$. Needing more than six trials means six consecutive failures, with probability at most $(1/2)^6=1/64$ under fresh independent choices, or under appropriately conditioned per-trial failure bounds. Reusing the same failed hash function gives the same placement, so repeated attempts are not independent trials and can fail forever. The expectation is not a deadline guarantee; rare long sequences remain possible. Recording the successful parameters makes final lookup deterministic even though construction used random retries.

title: Initialization included in perfect construction
stem: An accepted two-level first stage has $\sum_j\ell_j^2\le4n$. Each nonempty bucket needs at most two expected trials, each initializing and checking $\ell_j^2$ slots. Derive total expected second-stage work including initialization.
solution: For each bucket, expected work is at most a fixed constant times $2\ell_j^2$, absorbing placement/checking of its $\ell_j$ records because $\ell_j\le\ell_j^2$ when nonempty. Sum over buckets to get at most a constant times $2(4n)=8n$. This is linear expected total work and includes dense second-level initialization, unlike an unqualified one-level $n^2$ construction claim. Empty buckets contribute only bounded first-level metadata work. The accepted first-level space condition is crucial; without it the squared sum could be quadratic. Random construction and deterministic post-construction lookup remain separately stated properties.

title: Bloom-filter false positives
stem: A Bloom filter has 1000 bits, stores 100 keys and uses seven ideal independent bit hashes. Estimate false-positive probability and explain why this is not an exact dictionary membership result.
solution: The continuous estimate of a zero bit is $e^{-700/1000}=e^{-0.7}$. Approximate occupied-bit fraction is $1-e^{-0.7}\approx0.5034$, giving false-positive estimate $(1-e^{-0.7})^7\approx0.0082$. Exact zero-bit probability under independent draws is $(999/1000)^{700}$, but treating queried bit events as independent is an additional approximation. A positive response only means all requested bits are set, not that the key was inserted. Under an insertion-only correct implementation, an inserted key has no false negative because its bits remain set. Clearing shared bits for deletion breaks that property.

title: The Bloom-filter optimum
stem: For bit budget $b$ and $n$ keys, state the approximate optimum number of hashes and compute it when $b/n=8$. Compare the two neighboring integers and explain the computational tradeoff.
solution: The standard continuous false-positive approximation is minimized near $k=(b/n)\ln2$. At ratio eight this is about 5.545, so test integer choices five and six under the chosen approximation. They give roughly $(1-e^{-5/8})^5\approx0.0217$ and $(1-e^{-6/8})^6\approx0.0216$, with six slightly better. Every additional hash also adds work, so a practical choice can trade a small probability difference for throughput. The optimum is not a universal exact theorem for correlated hash outputs or a fixed finite bit layout. It depends on the idealized model and the absence of deletion errors.

title: A cuckoo capacity obstruction
stem: Four keys have candidate pairs drawn only from three slots: $(A,B),(B,C),(A,C),(A,B)$. Prove no one-key-per-slot placement exists. Does one cycle alone always imply failure?
solution: The four distinct keys have only three available candidate slots in their connected component. Pigeonhole immediately rules out placement. In the candidate graph, this component has four edges and three vertices, so it contains more keys than positions. A component containing exactly one cycle can still place its keys by orienting that cycle consistently and attaching tree edges away from it. Therefore observing a displacement cycle can indicate failure of a particular insertion path or trigger a bounded rebuilding policy without proving that every possible placement is impossible. The four-on-three example is a genuine structural obstruction, not merely an animation loop.

title: Two-sum with duplicate values
stem: Process $[4,1,4]$ for target eight using a prior-values hash set. Give the exact query/insert sequence and explain why inserting before querying can produce a wrong answer for input $[4]$.
solution: Initially the set is empty. For the first four, query complement four and miss, then insert four. For one, query seven and miss, then insert one. For the final four, query four and succeed because the first position already supplied that value. Two distinct positions form the pair. If the current value were inserted before its own complement query, the one-element input four would falsely match itself. The set stores values rather than positions, but the operation order enforces distinctness. Expected linear total work follows only with the table's expected lookup/insertion assumptions and safe arithmetic for computing the complement.

title: Prefix-sum counting
stem: Count zero-sum contiguous subarrays of $[2,-2,2,-2]$ using a frequency map of prior prefix sums. Give every update and total, including the initial empty prefix.
solution: Start frequencies with zero occurring once. The prefix sums are two, zero, two and zero. At prefix two, add its prior frequency zero and set its count to one. At zero, add one and raise zero's count to two. At the next two, add one and raise two's count to two. At the final zero, add two and raise zero's count to three. Total is four. The empty-prefix initialization counts subarrays starting at the first element. Query before incrementing prevents counting a zero-length subarray at the current position. Map updates replace counts; they do not create duplicate key records.

title: Ordered queries versus equality queries
stem: A service needs equality lookup, predecessor by key, key median and deletion of maximum priority, with priority unrelated to key order. Explain why one plain hash table is insufficient and outline a correct combined structure.
solution: A hash table routes by equality-oriented codes and does not preserve key or priority order. Predecessor and median cannot be inferred from neighboring physical slots. Maintain a balanced tree ordered by key with subtree sizes for rank selection and an aggregate identifying the maximum-priority record under a specified tie policy. An identifier map can locate records quickly. Priority changes update winner aggregates along the affected path; deletion changes both size and priority metadata. All mutation paths must maintain consistency. With balanced height, the ordered operations and aggregate maintenance take logarithmic worst-case tree work; hash lookup contributes its separately qualified expected cost.

title: A deterministic alternative under hostile hashing
stem: An application requires a worst-case logarithmic bound for arbitrary keys and ordered range queries. Should an expected constant-time chained table automatically be preferred? Give a justified selection.
solution: The requirements favor a balanced comparison tree with an appropriate key comparison operation. It supports ordered range/rank navigation and has a logarithmic worst-case height guarantee. A chained table may have faster typical equality lookup but permits a linear bucket and does not supply ordered range navigation. Combining structures can support both, yet adds memory and consistency work. The choice depends on required operations and guarantees rather than comparing unqualified “one” versus “logarithm” costs. If key comparisons inspect long strings, the tree's character cost must also be stated; worst-case node visits and total key-processing work are distinct measures.

title: A complete counter-and-correctness audit
stem: Audit this claim: “At load below one-half, every hash-map insertion is constant worst-case time; any deleted slot can terminate search; resizing only copies slots; equal hashes identify equal keys.” Give a precise replacement for each clause.
solution: Low load can support constant expected performance under a suitable random model but does not prevent concentrated chains or long linear-probing clusters. A deleted marker preserves reachability and must not terminate unsuccessful search; only a never-used/currently repaired empty slot provides that certificate. Resizing changes routes, so live records must be rehashed/reinserted and a triggering operation can be linear actual time. Equal hashes require an actual key-equality check; unequal keys can collide even with a good family. A valid map additionally handles duplicate updates without increasing live count and uses bounded routes. These corrections jointly restore both the contract and the cost qualifications rather than patching only one erroneous complexity label.
